chapter_title: Pharmacogenetics – A Treatment Strategy for Alcoholism
source_pdf: /mnt/project-files/Experimental Provenance for QSAR Dataset/Pharmacology (Luca Gallelli) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf

records.role_detail: book: blocks ALDH activity by forming intermolecular disulfide bridges
records.quote: The proposed mechanism of action of disulfiram on alcohol use has been found to be primarily related to the inhibition of liver aldehyde dehydrogenase
records.notes: Same paragraph also says 'It blocks ALDH activity by forming intermolecular disulfide bridges resulting in acetaldehyde accumulation.' The paragraph also names a secondary action 'via modulation of catecholamine neurotransmission' with no molecular target; not recorded separately. Quote spans a line break on the page.

records.role_detail: PDF page 257 adds: chelates copper and thus inhibits the copper containing enzyme
records.quote: In clinical doses, disulfiram inhibits the enzyme dopamine–β–hydroxylase, which converts dopamine to norepinephrine
records.notes: The exact dash glyphs around the beta in 'dopamine–β–hydroxylase' could not be confirmed from the page image (en dash assumed). On PDF page 257 the enzyme is printed 'dopamine beta hydroxylase' and 'DβH'.

records.quote: specifically through antagonism of the µ−opioid receptors
records.notes: The glyph between 'µ' and 'opioid' looks like a minus sign or dash; exact character not confirmed. PDF page 256 says 'µ OPRM1, which is the primary target of naltrexaone' (book's spelling). PDF page 254 also says 'Nalotrexane blocks the release of these endorphins' (book's spelling); no molecular target is named there, so it is not a separate record.

records.mechanism_book_wording: antagonizing of the N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor site or via modulation of glutamate neurotransmission
records.quote: The mechanism of action is through antagonizing of the N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor site or via modulation of glutamate neurotransmission
records.notes: The book offers this as one of two alternatives ('or via modulation of glutamate neurotransmission'). PDF page 257 mentions the NMDA receptor and 'glutaminergic mGLU5 receptor' in connection with acamprosate response, without a direction of action.

records.quote: Ondansetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist used mainly as antinausea medicine
records.notes: Book lists it under 'Other promising medicines', in clinical use; regulatory status not stated. PDF page 257 says 'Ondansetron, an antagonist of serotonin' and '5-HT3 receptor antagonist ondansetron'.

records.quote: Baclofen, a GABA B receptor antagonist is used clinically for the treatment of muscle spasticity
records.notes: Recorded exactly as printed: the page says 'antagonist'. Reader's remark, not from the page: baclofen is generally described elsewhere as a GABA B receptor agonist, so this statement in the book should be checked before use. Book says it is 'used clinically'; regulatory status not stated.

records.mechanism_book_wording: antagonizing α amino-3-hydroxy 5-methylisoxazole 4-propionic acid (AMPA) and kainate glutamate receptors
records.quote: Its action is mediated via antagonizing α amino-3-hydroxy 5-methylisoxazole 4-propionic acid (AMPA) and kainate glutamate receptors
records.notes: Book calls topiramate 'an antiseizure medication'; regulatory status not stated. 'amino-3-hydroxy' is split across a line break on the page ('amino-3-' / 'hydroxy').

records.mechanism_book_wording: antagonizing α amino-3-hydroxy 5-methylisoxazole 4-propionic acid (AMPA) and kainate glutamate receptors
records.quote: Its action is mediated via antagonizing α amino-3-hydroxy 5-methylisoxazole 4-propionic acid (AMPA) and kainate glutamate receptors
records.notes: Same sentence as the AMPA record. 'amino-3-hydroxy' is split across a line break on the page.

records.quote: as well as inhibition of GABA A receptors, L type calcium channels, and voltage dependent sodium channels (SCN)
records.notes: Recorded exactly as printed: the page says 'inhibition of GABA A receptors'. 'Antagonist' in the rule name is the nearer of the two receptor roles and is my mapping, not the book's word. Reader's remark, not from the page: this direction should be checked before use. Quote spans line breaks ('as' / 'well as').

records.quote: as well as inhibition of GABA A receptors, L type calcium channels, and voltage dependent sodium channels (SCN)

records.notes: The page names the process (serotonin reuptake), not a protein; 'transporter' as the target kind is my inference. Section heading reads 'Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI)'.

records.role_detail: book: acts on glycine binding site, inhibiting the function of NMDA receptor
records.mechanism_book_wording: act on glycine binding site therefore, inhibiting the function of NMDA receptor
records.quote: Alcohol has been reported to act on glycine binding site therefore, inhibiting the function of NMDA receptor
records.notes: Compound is ethanol, printed as 'Alcohol' here. The book's word is 'inhibiting the function'; 'Antagonist' in the rule name is my mapping to the nearer receptor role. Quote spans line breaks ('Alcohol has' / 'been reported').

records.quote: To open the channel of NMDA receptor, presence of glycine is required. Glycine is an amino acid which has its own site, acting as a coagonist.
records.notes: Book calls glycine 'an amino acid'; it does not use the words 'endogenous ligand'. Quote is two consecutive sentences, about 26 words.

records.target: L-type channels (L-type voltage sensitive calcium channels, VSCC)
records.quote: It has been found that alcohol (ethanol) blocks L-type channels.
records.notes: The sentence says 'L-type channels'; that they are voltage sensitive calcium channels (VSCC) comes from the preceding sentence on PDF pages 250-251. There are two spaces before 'It' on the page.

records.quote: The L-type VSCC antagonists show some ethanol, like effects in rats.
records.notes: Class named without a compound. 'VSCC' is expanded on PDF page 250 as 'Voltage sensitive calcium channels (VSCCs)'. The comma in 'ethanol, like' is as printed.

records.role_detail: inducer; book's word is 'induced (increase in activity up to 10 fold)'
records.mechanism_book_wording: CYP2E1 is induced (increase in activity up to 10 fold) by chronic alcohol drinking
records.quote: CYP2E1 is induced (increase in activity up to 10 fold) by chronic alcohol drinking
records.numbers_detail: 'increase in activity up to 10 fold' (PDF page 249); 'up to 10 fold' (PDF page 247)
records.notes: Borderline record: this is enzyme induction by chronic exposure, not direct activation. 'Activator' is the nearer of the two enzyme roles under the naming rule and is my mapping, not the book's word. A later reader may prefer to drop this record. PDF page 247: 'CYP2E1 is induced by high ethanol concentration and by chronic intake of alcohol or ethanol (up to 10 fold)'.

chapter_notes: Body text runs from PDF page 243 to the top half of PDF page 258; the reference list starts on PDF page 258 and runs to 266 (looked at, not extracted). The chapter has two figures and no tables; neither figure names a drug mechanism. Not recorded because the page gives no direction of action on a named target: glutamate at NMDA/AMPA/kainate receptors, alcohol at GABA A receptors, beta endorphin binding at the opioid receptor (OPRM1), disulfiram 'modulation of catecholamine neurotransmission', and acamprosate at the mGLU5 receptor. Two statements (baclofen as a GABA B receptor antagonist; topiramate inhibition of GABA A receptors) are recorded as printed and flagged in notes for checking.
